sp: Deborah Kirschner Vice President, External Relations, Prospect Park Alliance
p: constantly reminded of the climate crisis and its impact on New Yorkers’ lives. Parks, open spaces, and trees are vital to combatting stormwater and extreme heat. Moreover, public restrooms and outdoor drinking fountains in NYC Parks are vital amenities for residents and visitors. Having access to free, clean, safe, and accessible restrooms and fountains promotes visitor usage, quality of life, and public health. Increasing funding and staffing for NYC Parks is key to improving and maintaining park bathrooms and drinking fountains. When it comes to safety in our parks system, Parks Enforcement Patrol (PEP) Officers are an unarmed presence trained and equipped to address the range of potential safety issues in city parks. They offer first aid, provide crowd control, connect at-risk individuals with social services, and are authorized to issue summonses and arrests. NYLCV supports expanding this workforce to bring more stable, middle-class jobs for New Yorkers. As we approach the start of a new City Council session and the next Mayoral Administration, we hope elected officials will support Play Fair’s Parks 2030 Platform, a clear vision for a world-class parks system, and one that both the City Council and the Administration must make a priority. Too many parks remain understaffed, underfunded, and neglected, especially in communities that need them most. NYLCV looks forward to working with the current and future City Council, Mayor-Elected Mamdani, DPR, and park advocates to ensure we are investing in a world-class park system. Thank you for the opportunity to comment. 2

Written Testimony of Deborah Kirschner Vice President, External Relations, Prospect Park Alliance New York City Council Committee on Parks & Recreation Oversight Hearing on Parks Restrooms, Drinking Fountains, and PEP Coverage Monday, November 24, 2025 Chair Krishnan, members of the Committee, thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony for today's hearing. My name is Deborah Kirschner, and I serve as Vice President of Prospect Park Alliance, the nonprofit organization that partners with NYC Parks to care for Brooklyn’s Backyard, Prospect Park. Our team works alongside the agency every day, and we see firsthand the extraordinary dedication of Parks staff and the very real constraints caused by chronic underfunding and understaffing. Today’s discussion on the state of park restrooms, drinking fountains, and Parks Enforcement Patrol officers strikes at the heart of what makes public space accessible, equitable and essential for all New Yorkers. Parks are not amenities, they are essential infrastructure, especially in a city that depends on its parks as living rooms, backyards and cooling centers. Speaker Adams’ 2024 Nature’s Call: An Assessment of NYC Park Restrooms highlighted what many of us already know: too many restrooms and drinking fountains are in disrepair, closed during scheduled hours, or lacking basic safety and sanitary conditions. These outcomes are not the result of neglect by frontline staff. They are the predictable result of decades of disinvestment, and of a Parks workforce that simply does not have the capacity to maintain more than 1,400 restrooms and 3,700 drinking fountains citywide. Prospect Park is no exception. One of the restrooms included in the Council survey, the Willink Restroom at the Children’s Corner, illustrates the challenges faced by public facilities. This restroom serves some of the park’s most heavily visited family destinations, including the Carousel, the Zoo, and Lefferts Historic House. Yet after years of underinvestment, it has fallen into such disrepair that it becomes unusable during rain events. It has not undergone a major restoration since 1991. And through the support of the City Council, we are slowly raising the funds for its restoration. But as this example shows, restoring existing facilities—and much less expanding access as mandated by Local Laws 92 and 93—requires investment and staffing that the current Parks budget does not sustain. We see a similar strain when it comes to Parks Enforcement Patrol officers. Prospect Park sees its highest summer use, yet many PEP officers are reassigned to beaches during this same period. The result is fewer trained officers available during the busiest season, despite the fact that PEP officers are uniquely skilled in park rules, public engagement, and de-escalation. Our own correspondence from park users reflects a consistent desire for a fair and reliable level of coverage across parks and beaches alike.

Intro 1425 is an important step toward understanding these gaps. By requiring detailed, district-level reporting, the City will have clearer insight into where coverage falls short and where additional investment could make parks safer and more welcoming. The path forward is clear. New York City must invest in the staffing and resources needed to keep existing restrooms and fountains clean, functional, and open; to restore facilities like Willink; and to ensure adequate PEP officer coverage across all boroughs. These improvements can be realized quickly with targeted operating and maintenance funding—investments that will improve the daily experience of millions of New Yorkers. The Prospect Park Alliance stands ready to work in partnership with this Committee, NYC Parks, and our elected leaders to advance these goals. Together, we can ensure that the essential infrastructure of our parks reflects the dignity, health, and equity that every New Yorker deserves. Thank you for your time and leadership.

November 25, 2025 To the New York City Council, My name is Nijaah Howard, and I am the President of the Southeast Queens Dog Run Committee. I am writing today because, as a frequent user of our parks and as someone who advocates for the safety and well-being of our community, I have become increasingly concerned about the lack of security measures in our local parks — specifically around park bathrooms. As a resident and community leader, I often find myself needing to use the park bathrooms. However, the low lighting , lack of visible security presence , and absence of functioning cameras make these areas feel unsafe. I am an adult, and even I am hesitant to use these facilities. Recently, I learned of a deeply disturbing incident in which a woman captured footage of an adult male attempting to harm a child behind a park bathroom. Hearing this was a turning point for me. It confirmed what many of us already fear: poorly lit, unmonitored spaces create opportunities for dangerous behavior to go unnoticed. This is unacceptable — and preventable. I am urging the Council to prioritize and fund security cameras and improved lighting in and around park bathroom areas throughout Southeast Queens. These are not luxuries; they are essential safety measures. Our parks should be places where families, children, seniors, and everyday users can feel protected. Adding security cameras to the budget will help deter harmful behavior, support law enforcement when needed, and most importantly, reassure the community that their safety is being taken seriously. Our parks are vital spaces. They should not be places where anyone — especially children — is left vulnerable. Thank you for your time, your attention, and your commitment to public safety. I sincerely hope the Council will consider this request and take action to ensure that Southeast Queens parks are safe for all who use them.

Respectfully, Nijaah

Howard

New York City Council Committee on Parks & Recreation November 24, 2025 Improving the Maintenance of Park Bathrooms and Drinking Fountains Van Cortlandt Park Alliance Testimony Dear Councilmember Krishnan and Members of the Committee on Parks & Recreation: I am submitting this written testimony speaking for the staff and board of Van Cortlandt Park Alliance. We are a member of the Play Fair for Parks Coalition, which includes over 500 organizations from across the ﬁve boroughs. On behalf of the 3+ million people who use Van Cortlandt Park each year, we urge New York City to fund the repair and maintenance of public restrooms and drinking fountains in Van Cortlandt Park and all of NYC’s parks. The city must increase NYC Parks funding to repair damaged public restrooms and drinking fountains in parks and playgrounds, hire additional staff to ensure regular maintenance, and keep restrooms open later for the public. Van Cortlandt Park Alliance, the park’s recognized partner, often receives complaints that bathrooms and playgrounds are not open on time or closed too early . These problems are always due to lack of staff. NYC Parks maintains and operates over 700 public restrooms and 3,700 drinking fountains—the vast majority of public restrooms and fountains citywide, and more than any other city agency. These facilities are vital to public health, safety, and accessibility. Considering the chronic disinvestment in NYC Parks, we should be thanking Parks Department staff for their heroic efforts, not calling them to task . Any failure rests squarely on the shoulders of Mayor Adams who defunded parks during his tenure. Funding for staff and supplies to maintain bathrooms and water fountains needs to be baselined. It is time to stop yearly budget cuts that keep parks in crisis. Parks are critical infrastructure which have been overlooked and underfunded for the last 4 decades. Year after year, NYC Parks staff does more with less. The staff is already stretched too thin. They are tired and frustrated, and so are we. Van Cortlandt Park Alliance exists to help by adding supplemental programming and resources to the park, not to replace New York City funding. But that is now the role we ﬁnd ourselves in. In the summer of 2024, VCPA spent thousands of dollars to purchase garbage bags to keep the park clean, and toilet paper and hand soap to stock the park’s 7 public restroom buildings. Why isn’t the Parks budget funded at a level to supply these very basic items? Parks are essential to city life, providing equitable access to recreation for physical wellbeing, fresh air and open space for mental health, and a venue for much-needed social interaction. Parks need to be clean and safe in order to serve our great city. They should be funded and cared for accordingly. Christina Taylor Deputy Director Van Cortlandt Park Alliance

November 24, 2025 Honorable Shekar Krishnan New York City Council, District 25 250 Broadway, Suite 1816 New York, NY 10007 RE: Testimony to the New York City Council Hearing on NYC Parks Restrooms, Drinking Fountains, and PEP Officers Good morning My name is Gregory Christopher Baggett-Andrews, and I am testifying on behalf of the A. Philip Randolph Square Neighborhood Alliance and a resident of Central Harlem to urge the City Council to significantly increase funding for the repair, maintenance, and staffing of public restrooms and drinking fountains in our parks—particularly in Central Harlem and other heat island communities where these facilities are literally a matter of life and death. The Crisis in Central Harlem Central Harlem presents a deadly paradox. We are surrounded by five major historic parks—Central Park, Marcus Garvey Park, Morningside Park, St. Nicholas Park, and Jackie Robinson Park—yet Community District 10 has just 0.3 acres of parkland per 1,000 residents, Manhattan's lowest ratio and far below the citywide average of 1.8 acres. More critically, Central Harlem is a documented heat island with a heat island index of 5, the highest level of severity. On the same summer day last year, 126 West 126th Street, Suite 1405 New York City 10027 www.aprsquare.nyc (917) 406-9187 (mobile) friends@aprsquare.nyc

West 94th Street near Central Park measured 84 degrees while a treeless lot in East Harlem hit 115 degrees—a 31-degree difference. Central Harlem typically runs 10 degrees hotter than even East Harlem. Residents living in extreme heat islands like ours are twice as likely to die from heat stress as those in cooler neighborhoods. In this context, public restrooms and drinking fountains are not amenities—they are critical public health infrastructure. When water fountains run dry during heat waves and bathrooms are locked by 3 p.m., we are literally putting lives at risk. The State of Our Facilities NYC Parks maintains over 1,100 public toilets and 3,400 drinking fountains—more than any other city agency. These facilities should be sources of pride, ensuring public health, safety, and dignity for all New Yorkers. Instead, they tell a story of chronic disinvestment: ● A 2024 City Council survey of 100 park restrooms found two-thirds were closed during scheduled hours or had serious sanitary or safety issues ● Nearly 25% lacked baby changing stations ● 30% lacked garbage cans ● Council Member Brewer's 2025 survey documented widespread broken, unusable, or inaccessible drinking fountains In Central Harlem's small parks, squares, and playgrounds, which make up most of our green and open space, these conditions are even more severe. Our facilities receive minimal investment compared to flagship parks at our borders. With only 260 Parks Enforcement Patrol officers responsible for 30,000 acres citywide, safety personnel are virtually nonexistent in our pocket parks. Parks are operating with 1,000 fewer workers than in 2023, with 795 positions eliminated entirely. The results are visible every day: bathrooms locked by 3 p.m., overflowing trash, broken equipment unrepaired for months, and water fountains dry during heat waves—precisely when our community needs them most. The Cost of Inaction vs. The Cost of Solutions

We recognize that public bathrooms are expensive. Construction, maintenance, and enforcement are real obstacles. A single comfort station can cost millions to build and requires dedicated staff for cleaning, security, and repairs. These genuine challenges make the public facilities we already have in our parks even more pressing and urgent—especially in a community rated #5 as a heat island. We cannot afford to let existing infrastructure deteriorate while we debate building new facilities. Every locked bathroom, every broken water fountain, every unstaffed comfort station represents a failure to protect public health in communities already facing environmental injustice. Specific Needs in Central Harlem To address these inequities in Central Harlem specifically, we need: 1. Immediate repair and reopening of existing restroom and fountain facilities in Marcus Garvey Park, St. Nicholas Park, Jackie Robinson Park, and our neighborhood playgrounds 2. Extended operating hours for bathrooms—keeping facilities open until at least 8 p.m. during summer months when heat stress is most severe 3. Daily maintenance schedules with dedicated staff assigned to Central Harlem facilities 4. Emergency water access during heat advisories, including mobile water stations when fountains are under repair 5. Prioritization under Environmental Justice Zones that recognize Central Harlem's #5 heat island status 6. The One Percent Solution When Mayor-elect Mandani was asked by parks advocacy groups—including New Yorkers for Parks, the Urban Design Forum, and the Municipal Arts Society—he committed to dedicating 1% of New York City's budget to parks. Currently, our parks receive less than 0.6% of city funding, even though they cover 14% of New York's land.

If the city allocated 1% of the budget to parks, Central Harlem would benefit through: ● Staffing restoration: The $95 million needed to restore 1,000 park positions would enable staff to be on-site at heavily used restrooms during peak hours, addressing issues when they occur and keeping facilities open later ● Systematic repairs: Funding to address the backlog of broken fountains, damaged restrooms, and dysfunctional infrastructure throughout our small parks ● Preventive maintenance: Regular cleaning and inspection schedules that prevent facilities from deteriorating to unusable conditions ● Heat emergency response: Resources to ensure water access during the increasingly frequent and severe heat waves that threaten our community ● Evening programming: Staff to supervise facilities during evening recreation programs, making parks safer and more accessible for families Our Request We specifically call on the City Council to: 1. Allocate $25 million to hire 460+ additional NYC Parks workers responsible for cleaning, maintenance, and repair of park facilities, enabling staff presence at 400 heavily used restrooms during busiest times 2. Prioritize heat island communities like Central Harlem in the distribution of these resources, recognizing that working-class neighborhoods cannot supplement city funding with private conservancies 3. Support Intro 1425 to track PEP coverage by district, identifying staffing gaps and enabling more equitable resource allocation 4. Establish a timeline for bringing all existing Central Harlem park restrooms and fountains to full operational status before next summer 5. Champion the mayor-elect's commitment to allocate 1% of the city budget to parks

Conclusion Local Laws 92 and 93 require the city to add 50 drinking fountains and increase public restrooms to 2,120 within ten years. We cannot meet these goals while allowing existing facilities to crumble. In the climate crisis era, parks are frontline infrastructure. Public restrooms and drinking fountains are not luxuries—they are essential to public health, safety, and dignity. In Central Harlem, where extreme heat is already a documented public health emergency, they are matters of survival. Budget cuts fall heaviest on working-class neighborhoods like ours. While wealthier districts supplement city funding with private conservancies raising millions annually, Central Harlem depends entirely on public investment. We ask you to ensure that investment reflects our community's needs and our residents' right to the city. APPENDIX Budget Justification: Central Harlem's $3-4 Million Share of Parks Funding Central Harlem requires $3-4 million of the proposed $25 million parks allocation—approximately 12-16% of citywide resources. This estimate reflects five critical factors that compound our community's need: 1. Geographic Scope of Infrastructure Central Harlem borders five major historic parks—Central, Marcus Garvey, Morningside, St. Nicholas, and Jackie Robinson Parks—plus maintains dozens of neighborhood playgrounds, squares, and pocket parks. This represents 30-50+ restroom and fountain facilities requiring daily maintenance, security, and extended operating hours. Each facility needs coverage 12+ hours daily during summer months. 2. Staffing Requirements At approximately $54,000 per position (based on the $25 million creating 460+ jobs), properly staffing Central Harlem's facilities requires: ● 20 positions for major park boundaries ($1.08 million) ● 15 positions for neighborhood parks/playgrounds ($810,000) ● 10 positions for maintenance and emergency response ($540,000)

● 5 positions for evening/weekend coverage ($270,000) Total: 50 positions = $2.7 million baseline 3. Heat Island Emergency Multiplier As a #5 ranked heat island where residents are twice as likely to die from heat stress, Central Harlem cannot be funded at average levels. With temperatures running 10 degrees hotter than East Harlem and 31 degrees hotter than areas near Central Park, our water and restroom access is literally life-saving infrastructure. This health emergency justifies a 30-40% premium above baseline funding. 4. Equity Correction for Historic Underinvestment With just 0.3 acres of parkland per 1,000 residents—six times below the city average of 1.8 acres—Central Harlem starts from a massive deficit. Achieving equitable service levels requires proportionally higher investment to overcome decades of neglect. Our broken fountains and 3 p.m. bathroom closures reflect this chronic underfunding. 5. Zero Private Investment—100% Public Dependency This is the critical factor that distinguishes Central Harlem from other communities. While Central Park benefits from a conservancy that raises $70+ million annually, and Bryant Park operates on a $20 million private budget, Central Harlem has NO private conservancies, NO corporate sponsors, and NO supplemental funding. Every dollar for our parks must come from public investment. Wealthier neighborhoods effectively double or triple their parks budgets through private philanthropy. In Central Harlem, the city allocation IS the entire budget. When the city provides only baseline funding, it ignores that other communities are adding millions in private dollars on top. This creates a devastating inequality: wealthy areas get city funds PLUS private millions, while Central Harlem gets city funds alone. Final Calculation: ● Base staffing need: $2.7 million ● Heat emergency premium (30%): $810,000 ● Equity adjustment for historic deficit: $490,000 ● Total: $4 million

This represents just 16% of the $25 million request, yet serves a community facing Manhattan's worst parkland deficit, deadly heat island conditions, and zero private support. Without this investment, Central Harlem residents will continue facing locked bathrooms, dry fountains, and preventable heat deaths while neighboring communities enjoy pristine, privately-funded facilities. The $4 million is not a request for special treatment—it's the minimum required to provide basic public health infrastructure in a community that depends entirely on public funding for survival. Thank you for the opportunity to submit this testimony. Gregory C. Baggett Founder, A. Philip Randolph Square Neighborhood Alliance Co-thought leader, REVIVE Harlem Lane
